extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in psychology (especially humor and moral psychology), behavioral scientists interested in laughter and emotion
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conditions from the benign-violation theory describing when violations (including moral violations) are perceived as humorous. Summarizes three specific conditions that make a violation 'benign' and thus likely to elicit laughter/amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and amusement result from violations that are simultaneously seen as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central theoretical claim integrating disparate conditions that facilitate humor. The authors tested this hypothesis across five experimental studies (in moral-violation contexts) and argue the account is consistent with evolutionary accounts of laughter and explains humor across many domains. The hypothesis implies that a stimulus is likely to be humorous when it is appraised both as a violation (something wrong) and as benign (something acceptable or not harmful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an alternative norm
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of an alternative norm suggesting that the situation is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as condition (a) making a violation appear benign; if observers can invoke a different norm or framing that legitimizes the behavior, the violation is more likely perceived as benign and elicit humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak commitment to the violated norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak commitment to the violated norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as condition (b). When people do not strongly endorse or feel bound by the norm being violated, the violation is more likely to be experienced as benign and thus humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distance from the violation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as condition (c). Greater psychological distance (temporal, spatial, social, or hypothetical) makes violations seem less threatening and more benign, increasing the chance of amusement or laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambivalent appraisal mediates humor (wrong and not wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing a violation as both wrong and not wrong mediates behavioral displays of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports that perceiving a violation as simultaneously wrong and not wrong explains why benign moral violations elicit laughter and amusement in addition to negative emotions. This ambivalent appraisal is a mechanistic mediator between benign-violation perception and humorous behavioral responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral violations often elicit negative emotions (especially disgust)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong documented association between moral violations and negative emotions, particularly disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background empirical observation noted by the authors: moral violations typically produce negative affect. The benign-violation framework explains how humor can nevertheless accompany these violations (i.e., eliciting laughter alongside disgust) when the violation is appraised as benign.
